title: Fast and Slow Reactions
objective: After this level you can explain what speeds reactions up or slows them down.
summary: Particles react only when they collide with at least the activation energy. Heat, more surface and higher concentration make good collisions more frequent; cold slows reactions.

cards.headline: Same food, same kitchen. Why does the fridge buy you days?
cards.body: Leave food on the counter and it can spoil quickly. Put the same food in the fridge and it stays fresh for days. The spoiling reactions haven't changed; only their speed has. So what sets the speed of a reaction?

cards.headline: Reactions are collisions
cards.body: Particles can only react when they bump into each other. And not every bump counts: they have to meet the right way round and with enough energy. Chemists call that minimum energy the activation energy. Picture a crowded dance floor where only a solid, well-aimed high-five counts. Anything that makes good collisions more common speeds a reaction up.

mascot.line: Hold on to activation energy. Level 56's catalysts work by lowering it.

cards.headline: Turn up the heat
cards.body: Remember Level 4? Heat makes particles move faster. Faster particles collide more often, and more of them hit hard enough to clear the activation energy. For many reactions, a rise of just 10 °C roughly doubles the rate. Now run it backward and you have your fridge: colder food, slower particles, fewer successful collisions, slower spoiling.

cards.headline: Smaller pieces, faster reaction
cards.body: A solid can only react at its surface. Chop it into smaller pieces and far more surface is exposed. That's why a big log smolders, small sticks burn quickly and fine sawdust can burn explosively. Crowding in more reactant particles works too: a higher concentration usually means a faster reaction.

cards.headline: Reaction speed: controlled
learned: Particles must collide with enough energy: the activation energy
Heat speeds reactions; cold slows them
Smaller pieces expose more surface and react faster
Higher concentration usually means a faster reaction

questions.prompt: In collision theory, what is activation energy?

options.label: The heat a reaction gives off at the end
options.rationale: That is the reaction's energy output, not its entry fee.

options.label: The minimum energy colliding particles need to react
The energy a fridge uses to stay cold
options.rationale: Nothing to do with the fridge itself.

options.label: The speed of the fastest particle in a sample
options.rationale: It is an energy threshold for a collision.

questions.explanation: Colliding particles need at least the activation energy, and the right orientation, to react.

questions.prompt: Why does food stay fresh longer in a refrigerator than on the counter?

options.label: Cold stops every reaction completely
options.rationale: It slows them; it doesn't stop them.

options.label: The fridge removes the oxygen from food
Slower particles make fewer successful collisions, so spoiling slows
Cold air works as a catalyst

questions.explanation: Lower temperature means slower particles and fewer collisions that clear the activation energy.

questions.prompt: Sawdust and a log are the same fuel from the fire triangle. Why does the sawdust burn so much faster?

options.label: Sawdust exposes far more surface to oxygen
Sawdust is a different chemical from wood
options.rationale: It is the same wood in smaller pieces.

options.label: Logs contain no fuel inside
options.rationale: The whole log is fuel; most of it just isn't exposed.

options.label: Sawdust needs no heat to start burning

questions.explanation: Smaller pieces expose more surface, so far more fuel meets oxygen at once.
